chunks: And what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Abd al-Malik from Sulayman ibn Khalid, who said:

I asked him about a man who trod on the eggs of the sandgrouse (qatā) and crushed them. He said: He should send a male goat in number equal to the number of the eggs from the sheep, just as he sends a male goat in number equal to the count of the eggs from the camels. And whoever hits an ostrich egg, upon him is a young sheep (makhāḍ). There is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because a young sheep from the sheep is only obligatory by specification if there is a chick inside the egg, as we said regarding the eggs of the ostrah that a yearling camel (badanah) is obligatory if there are chicks inside it. And that which indicates that the ruling of the eggs of the sandgrouse is the ruling of the eggs of the ostrich.

key_terms.مَخَاضٌ: A young sheep (specifically one year old)

ai.seo_question: What is the compensation for crushing bird eggs in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration from Musa ibn al-Qasim to resolve apparent contradictions in the fiqh of bird eggs by distinguishing between eggs containing a developing fetus (farakh) and those that do not. This distinction is crucial in Shia jurisprudence for determining whether the compensation is a standard male goat (fahl) or a more valuable yearling camel (badanah), reflecting the principle that liability increases with the maturity of the offspring.
